title: When Does LLM-Extracted Central Bank Sentiment Add Value? A Fragility Analysis of Sentiment-Tilted CVaR Portfolios in FX Markets
abstract: This paper stress-tests a common claim in the emerging LLM-for-finance literature: that LLM-extracted sentiment can improve risk-based portfolio optimization. Using the full text of 45 FOMC statements (January 2021-July 2026), Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash model, IG Markets broker-executable daily prices, and official central-bank policy rates for carry, we construct a sentiment-tilted Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) strategy on six major USD currency pairs and subject it to a battery of robustness checks rarely applied jointly in this literature: a formal Sharpe-ratio equality test, a 500-permutation placebo test, eventlevel clustered inference with block and stationary bootstrap confidence intervals, a nested walk-forward procedure for selecting the tilt-strength parameter without look-ahead, a Minimum-Variance benchmark, a Loughran-McDonald dictionary comparison, pair-specific transaction-cost and FOMC-announcementwindow stress tests, and two stability probes-repeated LLM queries and substitution of three reproducible alternative model families (Llama 3.1 8B, GPT-OSS 120B, Qwen 3.6 27B). The central finding is fragility, not confirmation. The main specification shows a higher point-estimate Sharpe ratio (0.398 to 0.609) and Sortino ratio (0.494 to 0.877) than a sentiment-free baseline, but a Jobson-Korkie/Memmel test does not reject equal Sharpe ratios (p = 0.699; 95% CI for the difference: [-0.861, 1.285]), and the genuine signal falls at only the 78th percentile of the 500-permutation placebo null. Every stability probe degrades, reverses, or fails to confirm the result: re-running the backtest with the 10repetition mean polarity score in place of the single-pass score all but eliminates the Sharpe ratio (-0.001, against individual single-repetition Sharpe ratios ranging from 0.081 to 0.628) despite 0.979 correlation with the single-pass score; of three reproducible alternative model families, Llama 3.1 8B raises the Sharpe ratio to 1.063 while GPT-OSS 120B and Qwen 3.6 27B lower it to 0.300 and 0.157, and none is statistically distinguishable from the Baseline (Memmel p = 0.217, 0.861, and 0.669 respectively). A fourth model, Llama 3.3 70B, was deprecated by its provider before this specification was finalized and could not be reevaluated; its earlier point estimate (Sharpe = 0.153) is reported for completeness only. A look-ahead-free procedure for the tilt-strength parameter λ selects a positive tilt in 30 of 58 periods, yet the resulting out-ofsample Sharpe ratio (0.393) is statistically indistinguishable from a fixed no-tilt policy. Two comparisons complicate a purely negative reading, though not in the direction a diversification story would predict. A Minimum-Variance benchmark with no sentiment achieves a Sharpe ratio (0.336) below both the Baseline and the LLM-tilted strategy, so generic risk-minimization alone does not explain the apparent gain over the naive Baseline; the source of the Baseline's own advantage over pure varianceminimization is a question we do not resolve here. A Loughran-McDonald dictionary signal underperforms the baseline and turns the strategy's realized Sharpe ratio negative (-0.050) while the LLM signal outperforms it (Memmel p = 0.365)-consistent with genuine LLM-specific content, though the comparison itself is not statistically significant. We interpret the evidence as showing that LLM-extracted sentiment is highly sensitive to sampling variation, model choice, data source, and parameterization in ways a single point-estimate backtest cannot reveal, and propose this joint battery as a minimum robustness standard for future work.
why: LLM sentiment FX strategy, comprehensive robustness testing.

title: Do Capital-Goods Incentive Announcements Move Italian Industrial Stocks? An Event Study with LLM-Coded Regulatory Acts, 2019–2026
abstract: This paper asks whether the Italian stock market prices the acts of capital-goods incentive policy (Transizione 4.0, Transizione 5.0, Nuova Transizione 5.0) when they are issued, and whether a large language model (LLM) reading those acts can extract a signal that the market incorporates with a lag. A corpus of 37 legislative and administrative acts between April 2019 and June 2026 is coded manually and, independently and blind, by an LLM; concordance is near-complete on category and date, substantial on intensity and moderate on expected sign. A market-model event study on 30 directional events and a two-tier basket of eight Euronext Milan stocks (domestic users of incentivised assets and suppliers of eligible capital goods) finds no abnormal return after the event under any coding: signed CAAR of +0.09% on [+1, +5] and +0.39% on [0, +5] under the manual coding, both indistinguishable from zero; a publication-day estimate of +0.29% that does not survive multiple-testing correction, the Corrado rank test, the Kolari-Pynnönen cross-correlation adjustment, the clustering of overlapping acts or the LLM coding. The result holds at the political-announcement date, is robust to estimation windows, basket composition and a survivorship control, and has a minimum detectable effect of about 1.5%. A post hoc hypothesis that the direction of acts follows the sector cycle is rejected on machine-tool orders and on official Eurostat data: the direction of an act is explained by its administrative nature (industrial policy versus spending control). The contribution is a documented negative result on a source of unstructured open data not covered by the financial text-mining literature.
why: LLM regulatory coding, event study, no abnormal returns.

title: Agentic Decision Mathematics: Risk-Constrained Allocation of Operational Autonomy Under Uncertainty in Financial Market Infrastructure
abstract: This paper introduces Agentic Decision Mathematics-a deterministic computational architecture that interposes applied mathematics between large language model (LLM) agents and securities-operations execution systems. Rather than permitting an agent to decide and execute autonomously, the architecture maintains a Bayesian belief state over the operational situation, evaluates proposed actions against mathematical constraints, selects the optimal action via a risk-constrained objective function incorporating Conditional Valueat-Risk (CVaR), and authorises execution through formal gates. A central architectural principle is that the agent does not own the state of the world: the control layer maintains the operational belief state, and the agent may only propose an interpretation of the evidence. We decompose uncertainty into three distinct types-state uncertainty (what is happening operationally), model uncertainty (is the AI's interpretation correct), and outcome uncertainty (what happens if we act)-and integrate all three into a unified optimisation. Conformal prediction provides calibrated uncertainty sets over agent interpretations, while a Calibration Registry transparently exposes where statistical evidence is sufficient for autonomy and where it is not. The Autonomy Frontier classifies proposed actions along expected benefit, composite operational risk (incorporating reversibility, detectability, and propagation), and calibration quality-partitioning actions into autonomous, proposed, approval-required, and denied categories. The objective-function weights are treated as first-class governance objects, exposed through a Policy Sensitivity analysis that reveals where a decision is technically obvious and where it is a risk-appetite disagreement disguised as an AI question. Queueing-theoretic and graphtheoretic formulations address workforce optimisation under capacity constraints and bottleneck identification across end-to-end operational processes, explicitly modelling the non-linear relationship between processingminute removal and sustainable headcount reduction. The central formal contribution is the formulation of autonomy as a scarce, optimisable resource. We formulate the autonomy-allocation problem: given exception classes with arrival rates, resolution probabilities, risk profiles, calibration quality, and drift status, the optimal allocation of autonomy across classes maximises human work removed subject to a risk envelope, tail-loss constraint, calibration thresholds, and runtime-checked invariants. Existence of an optimal allocation is straightforward when the feasible set is non-empty (finite classes, discrete autonomy levels); the non-trivial open question is convergence under distributional drift. The paper positions this work within the emerging regulatory landscape, including the Monetary Authority of Singapore's SAFR framework and NIST guidance on continuous monitoring. The executive proposition: AI proposes. Mathematics decides what is permissible, optimal, and sufficiently certain. Controls decide whether it executes.
why: LLM operations governance, formal architecture.

title: Computation Is Explanation: An Active Inference Agent for Interpretable Portfolio Control
abstract: AI for portfolio management faces a structural explainability problem. Opaque models lack auditable pre-trade rationales, while transparent associational models can remain causally misspecified. We propose \emph{Finance-native Active Inference}, an ante-hoc interpretable portfolio control architecture. The agent is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) whose generative model decomposes each decision into regime beliefs, preferences, expected free energy, policy probabilities, and confidence-gated actions. The same objects that produce a trade also explain it; explanation is therefore part of the decision computation rather than a post hoc approximation. Surgical learning confines adaptation to exogenous market channels while freezing the endogenous profit and loss channel, mitigating a specific policy-feedback failure mode in adaptive financial models. We evaluate the framework using an event-centered design around the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) stress episode, walk-forward folds, and a cross-section of ten U.S.\ ETFs over 2015--2025. On the KBE bank ETF, adaptation reverses a frozen Sharpe ratio of $-0.76$ to $+0.84$, broadly matching the passive KBE benchmark while improving drawdown relative to the frozen agent. On SPY, frozen and adaptive modes produce identical positions, and across the ETF cross-section, adaptation improves Sharpe ratios in 8 of 9 non-tied frozen--adaptive comparisons. The contribution is a glass-box AI system for portfolio management that provides transparent, interpretable, and auditable adaptive control under non-stationarity while remaining explicit about its benchmark performance. The framework also offers practical guidance for AI model-risk governance by linking each decision to auditable beliefs, preferences, policy values, confidence gates, and validation artifacts.
why: Active inference portfolio agent, interpretable design.

title: Which Learned Forecaster Wins, and When? A Regime-and Horizon-Conditioned Comparison of Recurrent, Attentional, Generative and Tree-Based Stock-Forecasting Models, with a Regime-Switching Mixture of Experts
abstract: Deep and machine-learning forecasters have largely displaced classical models in the applied equity-forecasting literature, yet that literature cannot agree on which of them is best: recurrent, attentional, generative and tree-based architectures have each been reported as the strongest performer. We argue that this is not a failure of individual studies but a misconception of the target. Skill among learned forecasters is conditional-on the market regime, the forecast horizon, and the loss lens-so a scalar ranking estimates a quantity that is not stable, and the model that wins in one sample is not the model that wins in the next. We establish this directly and then exploit it. Four learned forecasters (an attention-pooled LSTM, a Transformer encoder, a TimeGAN-style adversarial model, and gradient-boosted trees) are implemented inside a single harness that fixes a 69-feature causal input substrate spanning returns, volatility structure, twenty-one technical indicators, cross-asset and macro-valuation context, market-based risk-appetite proxies and calendar effects; identical windowing; identical expanding-window walk-forward validation; and identical scoring. On 7,303 trading days of S&P 500 data (1990-2019) we show that the best learned forecaster rotates across folds and horizons-gradient boosting, then the LSTM, then the Transformer at one day; the adversarial model, then the Transformer, then the LSTM at five-so no single architecture can be selected ex ante. We then introduce a Regime-Switching Mixture of Experts (RS-MoE) that combines the learned forecasters through a hierarchically shrunk gate driven by the strictly causal, filtered posterior of a three-state Gaussian hidden Markov model, fit on pooled validation data from all prior folds. RS-MoE records 32 statistically significant wins and no significant losses against the four learned forecasters across horizon and regime buckets after Holm-Bonferroni adjustment, and at five-and twenty-day horizons it beats the ex post best learned model outright-by 0.36% and 7.41% of RMSE-without needing to know in advance which model that would be. It is also two to eight times more stable run-to-run than the stochastic experts it combines. The learned gate is interpretable and shifts weight from the short-horizon attentional and tree experts toward the parsimonious linear expert as the horizon lengthens. We report throughout, and do not conceal, that classical baselines-ARIMA and a random walk with drift-remain unbeaten in aggregate point error; we argue this is the correct scientific context for the result rather than a qualification of it, since the contribution is a solution to the model-selection problem among learned forecasters, which is where the field's disagreement actually lives.
why: Regime-conditioned forecaster selection; updates prior on model choice.

title: Delegated Consumption and the Missing Discipline of Competition An Equilibrium Theory of the AI Token Market
abstract: The unit price of artificial intelligence is collapsing, yet the price buyers pay per completed task has stopped falling. In the panel of Zhu (2026), quality-adjusted per-token prices fell at 0.73 log points per year over 2025-2026 while the per-task buyer price stood still. We trace this scissors divergence to delegated consumption. Once AI services execute tasks autonomously, the firm controls both the posted price per token, open to undercutting, and the per-task consumption intensity, which no standardized, audited measurement lets a buyer verify. In a duopoly model in which buyers perceive each firm's consumption only at a discount 𝜓 toward a market reference level, competition yields four results. The per-token markup vanishes; consumption stalls at a perception floor independent of competitive intensity and strictly above first-best; the buyer's pertask bill converges to a floor above efficient cost; and raising 𝜓 repairs the wedge continuously. Whenever the curvature elasticity of the quality technology is below one, the per-task bill rises as tokens get cheaper, an efficiency paradox in which every gain arrives as deeper consumption. We recompute the three headline indices of Zhu (2026) to published precision, measure consumption intensity as a large unpriced design variable, and preregister a two-arm design for runtime drift. The results speak to metering standards, disclosure regulation, and tariff design.
why: AI token pricing economics: explains why per-token prices collapse but per-task prices stall. Real market phenomenon, duopoly model explains mechanism

title: Machine Learning for Cross-Sectional Return Prediction: A Comparative Study of US and Indian Equities
abstract: Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020) showed that machine learning can improve cross-sectional stock return prediction by capturing nonlinear relationships between firm characteristics and future returns. This study applies a simplified version of their framework to 60 US and 60 Indian large-cap stocks using 27 price and volume characteristics. Four models (Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and a neural network) are evaluated using expanding-window walk-forward validation, producing 35 out-of-sample test months in each market. None of the models produces statistically significant portfolio returns at the 5% level in either market. Model rankings also differ across the two markets: Ridge performs best in the US, while the neural network performs best in India. Two patterns appear consistently in both markets. Small portfolio legs (six stocks each, given the 60-stock universe) can be strongly affected by a few extreme individual stock returns, and a model's point-prediction accuracy does not always correspond to its portfolio performance. These findings show why machine learning models should be evaluated using both prediction metrics and portfolio outcomes. The results should be treated as exploratory, given the small universe size and short out-of-sample period.
why: Small-cap ML no alpha, negative result rigorous.

title: The Algorithmic Fiduciary: A Cross-Jurisdictional Formal Model of AI-Mediated Disruption of Market Failures in Personal Financial Advisory Markets
abstract: Personal financial advice markets across developed economies exhibit five interconnected failures: information asymmetry, principal-agent conflicts, credence-good evaluation problems, shrouded product attributes, and licensing-induced exclusion. Drawing on evidence from Canada, Germany, India, Sweden, the Netherlands, and the United States, we develop a unified formal framework showing that artificial intelligence advisory systems restructure the equilibrium conditions underlying each failure, and prove that the welfare channels are complementary rather than additive. Calibrated to recent robo-advisory evidence, cumulative gains reach 2.5-3.0% of assets under management annually, falling to 1.07-1.95% once adoption constraints bind. Because adoption is governed by generalized trust, which varies substantially across countries, we show that identical AI capability yields materially different realized welfare across jurisdictions. We analyze how three divergent regulatory regimes - the US rules-based approach, the UK outcomes-based Consumer Duty, and the EU AI Act's risk classification - condition these gains, and derive six policy recommendations including a computational fiduciary standard.
why: Robo-advisor welfare; cross-jurisdictional formal model.

title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow
abstract: Classical market-making strategies based on stochastic control, such as the Avellaneda-Stoikov and the Guéant-Lehalle-Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) extension, provide closed-form quoting rules, but rest on assumptions that break down at realistic microstructure timescales. One of them is that order flow is stationary, while empirical evidence points to the existence of regimes, possibly associated with algorithmic execution of metaorders. In this case, existing methods provide negative PnL. In this paper, we develop a deep reinforcement-learning market maker (RLMM)-a Rainbow-style distributional DQN (C51) which is calibrated and tested in a zero-intelligence limit order book. We find that, in the stationary setting, RLMM outperforms GLFT across the entire observed risk-return frontier. The RLMM is more robust to flow asymmetry than GLFT, but, like any stationarily trained strategy, it still suffers large drawdowns from inventory saturation under persistent directional imbalance. Augmenting the state of RLMM with two auxiliary signals-a Bayesian online change-point filter over the directional flow bias and a queue-adjusted quote-exposure imbalance-restores profitability. A final scenario-bandit step that reweights low-return regime scenarios further improves performance under random-persistence and correlated-direction stress.
why: Rainbow DQN market maker vs Avellaneda-Stoikov in queue-reactive simulator. Real microstructure benchmarking but simulated not real data

title: A Safety Gate for AI-Driven Data Repair in Regulated Financial Reporting: Escalating Only the Fixes That Could Materially Misstate a Reported Figure
abstract: Financial institutions are increasingly automating data-quality controls and remediation workflows for the upstream inputs that feed regulated figures (loan-loss allowances, capital ratios, liquidity metrics). Newer AI and agentic tools are beginning to assist with anomaly investigation, repair recommendations, and workflow orchestration; for material regulatory-reporting inputs, however, production changes typically remain constrained by reconciliation controls, model-risk governance, and human approval gates rather than being fully autonomous. Existing repair systems, and the benchmarks that evaluate them, optimize for error reduction: how many broken values get fixed. We argue that in a regulated reporting context this is the wrong objective. The binding risk is not an inconsistent table; it is a reported figure that is wrong by a material amount, applied without human authorization. The method is regime-agnostic, applying to any additively-decomposable regulated figure such as a loan-loss allowance under CECL, regulatory capital under Basel, or a liquidity metric; we use a CECL allowance as the worked example. We formalize a repair-safety property for automated correction of such figures: a repair is admissible, meaning safe to auto-apply, only if it is reconciliation-preserving and cannot move any reported figure across its materiality threshold. We give a deterministic verification gate that auto-applies admissible repairs and escalates the rest, and prove it complete: no repair capable of a material misstatement or a control-total breach is ever silently applied. We show that completeness requires two conditions a naive gate omits, a non-finite-effect precondition and cumulative (not per-repair) materiality accounting, and that omitting either reintroduces silent material misstatements. We release matrepair, a reusable benchmark with a synthetic regulatory-aggregate generator, fault injection with ground truth known by construction, and three scoring axes (repair-safety, reconciliation-to-control-total, and materiality-tiered prioritization). On a stylized CECL allowance instance, an unguarded agent silently misstates the reported allowance in every configuration tested (agent error rates 0-50%, 200-800 faults); the gated pipeline silently misstates it in none, while still auto-applying the immaterial majority of repairs. The gate is orthogonal to, and composes with, existing agent-guardrail mechanisms: it contributes the property regulated repair requires, which those mechanisms cannot express. We scope the completeness result to additively-decomposable figures (sums, subtotals, and weighted sums, the dominant form of regulatory aggregation) and give a Lipschitz-bounded extension for non-decomposable figures such as ratios that preserves completeness at the cost of extra escalations, which we leave to empirical follow-up.
why: Real governance problem: materiality gates for automated data repair. No empirical validation or trading application

title: Where May the Model Sit? A Task-Position Framework for Governing Algorithmic Delegation in ERP-Integrated Financial Automation
abstract: Smaller organisations can now assemble a capable financial analysis workflow from an opensource enterprise resource planning system, a visual workflow automation platform and a metered interface to a general-purpose language model. Cost no longer selects which organisations possess such a capability. This paper argues that research treating generative artificial intelligence as a technology organisations adopt mislocates the governance problem that follows, and proposes task position within the workflow as the appropriate unit of analysis. Drawing on delegation theory as developed for information systems, it classifies tasks along two dimensions, determinism requirement and verification cost, and derives four delegation regimes. One regime is a prohibition rather than a conditional permission: tasks combining a single correct answer with costly verification are those in which delegation is least defensible and most tempting, because reliance there is never disciplined by observed error. A design principle operationalises the prohibition without requiring managers to reason about model internals, namely that no figure entering a financial report may originate in a language model. The paper specifies a four-layer control architecture and a minimum delegation record, and states seven falsifiable propositions. A secondary contribution distinguishes applicationprogramming-interface orchestration from the interface-level automation existing frameworks describe, arguing that the greater robustness of the former is what makes the governance problem urgent.
why: ERP automation delegation framework, practical governance.

title: Market Making via Reinforcement Learning Under Simulated Market Impact: A Queue-Reactive Reassessment of Spooner et al
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful tool that has much potential in the financial markets. In Spooner et al.’s Market Making via Reinforcement Learning, varying configurations of RL agents are trained and evaluated on historical order book data. However, this historical order book does not allow for market impact, nor is it easily generalizable for robust testing. To address this, we investigate the RL agent configuration of Spooner in a simulated order-book environment. We use a Zero-Intelligence model as a control, and then a Queue-Reactive model as a more realistic environment with market impact. The total PnL, mean absolute position, and trading behavior of the agents is then evaluated. In the Queue-Reactive simulator, the basic agent is essentially inactive (0.0 fills/episode) while the consolidated agent trades meaningfully more (33.0 fills/episode) yet still keeps its mean absolute position near zero (0.01, versus 0.00 for the basic agent). This suggests that, even under simulated market impact, the consolidated agent’s richer state representation lets it trade far more actively than the basic agent while still keeping its own inventory close to zero, echoing the inventory-management advantage Spooner reports for the historical order book.
why: RL market maker in queue-reactive simulator vs Avellaneda-Stoikov. Real microstructure but simulated not real LOB

title: From Dispute to Fait Accompli: In-System Financial Recoverability in Agentic Stablecoin Payments
abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents are beginning to search, compare, negotiate and initiate payments. Stablecoins and programmable settlement systems are being developed as always-on rails for machine-speed commerce. Existing debate asks whether an agent can be authorised to pay and whether its mandate can be bound to a transaction. This paper argues that the deeper governance problem is recoverability: the capacity of a payment arrangement to keep erroneous, manipulated or disputed financial action observable, contestable and supported by a practical remedial path before the dispute is forced outside the arrangement. Recoverability is neither a general right to reverse settlement nor a synonym for consumer protection. It is the institutional layer between authorisation and external legal recourse. Commercial-state compression, in which distinct states such as intent, authority, payment and fulfilment are collapsed into complete status claims, is one upstream mechanism by which agentic systems can weaken that layer; programmable settlement can then harden the error at machine speed. Closest technical work already addresses mandate binding, verified execution, provisional settlement, appeals and post-settlement auditability. The contribution here is comparative and institutional: to ask whether those mechanisms culminate in accessible, enforceable and financially credible remedies across the whole payment arrangement, including after final settlement or provider failure. Using card, account-based, wire and stablecoin arrangements, the paper distinguishes recoverability from finality and proposes risk-tiered release controls, claim and compensation windows, evidence-before-release, typed commercial-state objects, first-payer reimbursement and rebuttable loss allocation tied to control over the failed recoverability function. The objective is not to restore legacy friction, but to engineer its institutional replacement.
why: Stablecoin payment governance, real problem.

title: Transformer-Augmented Local Stochastic Volatility
abstract: Local stochastic volatility (LSV) models are widely used because they combine a stochasticvolatility state process with a leverage function calibrated to the current vanilla option surface. This paper investigates whether Transformer-based learning can improve the forecasting dynamics of a calibrated Local Stochastic Volatility (LSV) model. We first construct and independently validate an SPX LSV benchmark using an SSVI-Dupire local-volatility surface, a Heston-type stochasticvolatility backbone, and daily leverage-function calibration. We then compare three approaches: calibrated LSV, a temporal Transformer with a diffusion scenario decoder, and an LSV-conditioned Transformer. Neural models are trained exclusively on the pre-COVID development sample and evaluated on 616 daily OOT origins from July 2021 to December 2023. At the three-day horizon, the hybrid reduces Continuously Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) relative to LSV by approximately 42% for 30-day skew, 44% for 30-day curvature, 28% for 30-90-day forward skew, and 42% for forward curvature, while also outperforming the standalone Transformer. Economic relevance is assessed through one-month ATM-straddle hedging, where daily hedge-error RMSE performs better for the transformer augmented model. The results suggest that exact calibration to the current volatility surface can be improved upon for subsequent smile dynamics. Historical attention-based learning materially improves forecasts of skew and curvature, while conditioning on LSV structure provides additional predictive information beyond a standalone Transformer. There is a case for historical attention-based learning adding information about skew and curvature dynamics. We state the data, numerical assumptions, acceptance criteria and required next tests explicitly in this paper.
why: Transformer augments LSV for options: proper OOT on 616 dates, but incremental technical contribution

title: Spatiotemporal Signals in Residuals: A Two-Stage Boosting Graph Neural Network for Stock Return Prediction
abstract: Stock-return prediction remains challenging because financial markets are noisy, nonstationary, and characterized by dependencies that evolve across assets and time. LightGBM can capture nonlinear relationships between engineered quantitative factors and future returns, providing a strong tabular baseline, but it does not explicitly model coupled temporal and cross-sectional dependencies. We propose STB-GCRN, a two-stage residual-learning framework that augments this baseline with multi-source spatiotemporal information. The first stage generates baseline predictions and chronological out-of-fold residual targets. The second stage constructs quarterly updated relation graphs from industry classifications, valuation characteristics, and historical price movements, and learns residual corrections from these graphs and availability-aligned raw feature sequences. Learnable graph fusion, a shared spatiotemporal encoder, and relation-specific refinement branches model both common and view-specific dependencies. Under the reported evaluation protocol on the CSI 1000 and CSI 2000 universes, STB-GCRN improves IC, ICIR, gross annualized long–short return, and Sharpe ratio over LightGBM. On the CSI 1000, IC increases from 0.0708 to 0.0775 and ICIR from 0.5437 to 0.6432 . Ablation results associate the gains with the complementary relation sources and the two GCRN components. These results provide a new perspective on stock-return prediction by enabling prediction-correction learning for multi-factor models and facilitating their effective integration with spatiotemporal models.
why: Graph networks for returns; industry and valuation signals.

title: Firm Characteristics and the Cross-Sectional Variation in Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
abstract: This paper explores which characteristics of a given firm have predictive power over the magnitude and persistence of post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) using both a machine learning framework and linear regression approach. Using Compustat quarterly fundamentals and CRSP daily returns for a sample of 6,728 U.S. firms over 2004 to 2023, we construct a panel of 203,764 firm-quarter earnings events and compute cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) over 21 and 63 trading-day post-announcement windows. Standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) are measured via a seasonal random walk model. We then train a LightGBM gradient boosted model alongside an OLS ridge regression in a walk-forward validation framework, predicting 1 month post-announcement drift from 13 firm characteristics. The gradient boosted model achieves an out of sample R^2 of 1.04%, generating a predicted Q5-Q1 portfolio spread of 4.29% over 21 trading days, exceeding the raw SUE-sorted spread of 3.27%; in calendar-time long-short portfolios this spread is statistically significant (Newey-West t-statistic of 19.3 across 60 quarterly cohorts). Short term pre-announcement momentum, book-to-market ratio (BTM ratio), and intermediate momentum are the strongest predictors of drift magnitude, while SUE itself ranks ninth, suggesting that how a firm arrives at an earnings surprise matters more than how large the surprise is. The LGBM model (interchangeably referred to as the gradient boosted or machine learning model) substantially outperforms the linear baseline (interchangeably referred to as the OLS model or ridge regression model, R^2 of-0.0003), indicating that the predictive relationships are fundamentally nonlinear.
why: Low-signal PEAD, no transaction costs discussion.

title: From Efficiency Inflation to Judgment Density: A Measurement Framework for AI-Augmented Knowledge Work
abstract: Generative and agentic AI have sharply reduced the marginal cost of producing professional outputs, making baseline reports, presentations, code, summaries, and plans faster and more abundant. Prior work introduced efficiency inflation as a value-dilution mechanism and judgment density as the human contribution that preserves value when ordinary output becomes abundant. The present paper narrows that theory-building argument to a measurement problem: how can judgment density be observed, scored, calibrated, and eventually validated in AI-augmented knowledge work? The paper provisionally models judgment density as a formative measurement framework rather than a reflective psychological scale. It specifies five observable dimensions: J1 Problem Definition, J2 Context and Evidence, J3 Choice and Tradeoffs, J4 Risk and Boundaries, and J5 Responsibility and Defensibility. Ratings are anchored in observable judgment events-such as explicit assumptions, evidence trails, rejected alternatives, escalation conditions, and accountable decision ownership-rather than surface polish, verbosity, or whether AI was used. A three-phase validation agenda is proposed: (1) content-domain review and rater calibration, including inter-rater reliability assessment; (2) a blinded 2 x 2 construct-discrimination experiment that independently manipulates surface quality and judgment quality; and (3) an eight-week organizational field test linking J1-J5 profiles to structural rework, first-pass acceptance, material-error incidence, decision adoption, and decision time. The paper does not claim that judgment density is already a validated scale. Its contribution is a falsifiable measurement architecture that moves the Efficiency Inflation research program from conceptual explanation toward empirical testing and organizational application.
why: Judgment density framework, conceptual not grounded.

title: The Banking Fraud Landscape in Dual-Agency and Digital-Capability Perspectives
abstract: This study examines the structural evolution of U.S. financial institution crime from 2020 through 2025, evaluating how post-pandemic liquidity programs and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have redefined banking risk paradigms. Integrating Principal-Agent Theory (Jensen & Meckling, 1976) with the Fraud Diamond framework (Wolfe & Hermanson, 2004), we formulate a dual-agency model to analyze how digital capabilities expand traditional information asymmetry between internal management and external third-party digital actors. We demonstrate that bad actors exploit technological capability-rather than static insider access-to execute large-scale automated deception across high-velocity digital payment rails. Our analysis reveals key internal control mechanisms and vulnerabilities: distressed institutions manipulate Inline XBRL (iXBRL) tagging structures and disclosure granularity to obscure balance-sheet stress from automated regulatory screens (Blankespoor et al., 2014). Simultaneously, external actors deploy deepfakes, synthetic identities, and automated scripts to execute Authorized Push Payment (APP) scams. These dynamic strategies bypass traditional static Internal Controls over Financial Reporting (ICFR) and rules-based continuous auditing heuristics (Vasarhelyi et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2018). We evaluate these theoretical dynamics through four major regulatory enforcement actions (U.S. v. Bank of America Securities, Inc.; U.S. v. Andrew Hoang Do; U.S. v. Rafael Alvarez; and merchant processing ACH indictments), which highlight critical control failures across algorithmic trade monitoring, emergency liquidity controls velocity, source record falsification, and automated settlement rails. We conclude by presenting an empirical research agenda focused on adaptive AI-driven ICFR architectures under PCAOB AS 2401, computational linguistics for iXBRL disclosure analytics, and behavioral governance in decentralized operating environments.
why: Financial crime analysis, descriptive framework only.

title: The Control Gap: Capital Flows, Commodity Cycles, and Institutional Readiness for AI-Enabled Macroprudential Policy in Emerging Economies
abstract: This book examines a systematic gap in three decades of research by Chilean economist Andrés Fernández (IMF, former Head of Research at the Central Bank of Chile) on capital controls, commodity-driven business cycles, and firms' financial vulnerability in emerging economies. While this body of work has produced rigorous measurement tools — including the widely used FKRSU capital control dataset and, more recently, the use of large language models to reconstruct historical capital-flow restrictions — it does not address the institutional capacity of regulators to execute policy using equivalent AI-enabled tools in real time. The book proposes a four-dimension AI-Governance Readiness framework (data infrastructure, internal analytical capacity, enabling regulatory framework, and institutional response speed) specific to the macroprudential and capital-flow-management function, extending the institutional-readiness research program developed in the author's previous volumes (The Compliance Gap; The Adaptation Gap). This is a conceptual and methodological volume; empirical validation with real-world data is left to a planned companion volume.
why: AI governance framework, policy-focused study.

title: Innovation for Sustainability: Does Green Innovation Explain the ESG Returns to R&D Investment?
abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance has become a strategic priority for firms seeking sustainable competitiveness. However, the mechanisms through which research & development investment contributes to ESG performance remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates whether green innovation mediates the relationship between research & development investment and ESG performance using an unbalanced panel of 1,444 Chinese A-share listed firms from 2007 to 2022. Fixed-effects models, instrumental variable estimation, and system generalized method of moments are employed to address unobserved heterogeneity and endogeneity. To further strengthen the robustness of the findings, Bayesian regression, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, random forest analysis, bootstrap mediation tests, and quantile regression are incorporated as complementary analytical approaches. Our results indicate that research & development investment significantly promotes both green innovation and ESG performance, while green innovation exerts a positive effect on ESG performance and partially mediates the impact of research & development investment. The Bootstrap analysis confirms the statistical significance of the indirect effect. Bayesian inference and machine learning analyses provide consistent evidence supporting the robustness of the estimated relationships. The Quantile regression further reveals substantial distributional heterogeneity, with the contribution of green innovation being more pronounced among firms with relatively lower ESG performance. Additional heterogeneity analyses demonstrate that the complementarity between research & development investment and green innovation is stronger in heavily polluting industries than in non-heavily polluting industries. This study extends the literature by integrating conventional econometric methods with Bayesian inference and machine learning techniques to provide more comprehensive evidence on research & development–green innovation–ESG nexus. Our findings offer important managerial and policy implications for enhancing corporate sustainability through innovation-driven strategies.
why: Panel study 1,444 Chinese firms: robust methods (FE, IV, BART, RF) but ESG/sustainability focus not trading

title: Informed Investors and Corporate AI Innovation:,Evidence from Institutional Investors’ Corporate Site Visits
abstract: We examine whether institutional investor site visits facilitate corporate artificial intelligence (AI) innovation. Using site-visit records for Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, we find that more intensive institutional investor visits are associated with significantly greater subsequent AI patent applications and grants. The results are robust to alternative measures of site visits and AI innovation, more stringent fixed effects, entropy balancing, alternative sample restrictions, and an instrumental-variable approach based on the external research activity of visiting institutions. Mechanism tests suggest that site visits promote AI innovation by alleviating information frictions and mitigating managerial myopia. More intensive investor–firm communication and greater investor attention to AI-related issues are also associated with stronger subsequent AI innovation. The positive association is more pronounced among firms with greater human-capital and technological absorptive capacity. We further show that site visits improve the efficiency with which AI-specific investment is converted into AI patenting outcomes. Overall, our findings highlight institutional investor site visits as an important form of active capital-market engagement that supports firms’ development of knowledge-intensive general-purpose technologies.
why: Institutional investor site visits → corporate AI patents, corporate governance not trading

title: AI Analysts and the Changing BI Labor Market: A Review of Database Agents and Analyst Workflows
abstract: This paper examines labor substitution in agentic artificial intelligence for data science. The central issue is the changing boundary between tasks that can be substituted, tasks that are better augmented, and tasks that should remain human-led. We argue that the important shift is not that language models can write isolated snippets of code, but that agentic systems can bind intent clarification, tool use, iterative execution, error recovery, evidence synthesis, and stakeholder-facing explanation into one operational loop. This creates economic value by reducing coordination costs and expanding analytical capacity, yet it also changes the risk profile of data work: mistakes become more procedural, more compositional, and sometimes harder to detect. We develop a framework that treats the agent as an accountable analytical operator, evaluate implications for organizations, and propose design principles for robust deployment.
why: Labor substitution analysis, not financial methodology.

title: The $3 Trillion Question: A Macroeconomic Analysis of the AI Debt Market in 2029
abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic implications of the projected $3 trillion to $7 trillion AI-related debt market by 2029, analysing the structural transformation of corporate financing, financial stability risks, and broader economic consequences. Drawing on recent analyses from the Bank for International Settlements, industry research firms, financial institutions, and academic research, this study argues that the AI debt wave represents a paradigm shift in technology sector financing comparable to historical infrastructure buildouts. The analysis identifies four key macroeconomic channels: the transition from equity to debt financing, the creation of new asset classes, the concentration of credit risk, and the potential for a destabilising investment correction. The paper concludes that while the AI debt market could become a significant component of global credit markets, its sustainability depends critically on the commercial viability of AI applications and the resolution of structural bottlenecks in energy and semiconductor supply chains. Particular attention is paid to the opacity of private credit markets and the reflexive nature of AI infrastructure financing, where commitments sustain valuations that in turn enable further borrowing. A specific parallel is drawn between the current AI debt complex and the subprime securitisation crisis of 2007-2008.
why: AI debt analysis, no new methodology proposed.

title: Calibrating AI Automation and its Labor Market Impacts, Preliminary and Incomplete
abstract: We are early in the latest AI technological revolution, and there are vastly different projections circulating about the impact of AI on the labor market; most of these projections assume labor automation happens on a fixed schedule. I revisit this question by calibrating a model where labor automation is an endogenous outcome driven by the accumulation of AI capital. The speed of accumulation of AI capital is calibrated based on hyperscalers' and data-center investment. The model has an intelligence sector, composed of intelligence industries, where AI capital represents a (small) share of the sector's capital; this sector automates labor as more AI capital becomes available. The physical sector, composed of the rest of the industries, uses ordinary labor and capital, and does not have the option to automate labor. As AI capital grows, the intelligence sector automates, and workers quit into unemployment. Workers eventually find a job in the physical sector, where physical capital starts to grow in order to respond to the increased labor supply that raises its marginal productivity. The model incorporates three frictions: unemployment, a cap on physical capital investment rate, and an adoption friction for AI. I calibrate the model to the 2024 US economy. If AI capital grows through a series of limited booms, unemployment increases by at most 1.4 percentage points over 20 years. Even if AI capital keeps doubling every year, as assumed in the aggressive scenario of the central case, there is no increase in unemployment in the first two years, consistent with limited effects observed on unemployment so far. Unemployment then increases by 8.4 percentage points after 7 years, while average worker labor income (including zero income for the unemployed) decreases by 5.8%, and the labor share decreases by 13 percentage points. After automation in the intelligence sector completes (year 7), leaving only strictly necessary workers there, unemployment decreases, wages increase sharply (+47.5% at 10 years), and the labor share overshoots its initial value. Without frictions, labor income instead rises monotonically. Across plausible parameter values, the depth of the income trough and the size of the ten-year wage gain depend most strongly on the growth rate of AI capital; most other parameters play a smaller role. This pins both automation and labor market effects to the growth rate of AI capital, which is therefore a key variable to watch.
why: Theory not empirically validated, endogenous automation.

title: AI-mediated Business Readiness: A Conceptual Framework for Business Discovery, Selection, Transaction, and Delivery in AI-mediated Markets
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming an intermediary between customers and businesses. Whereas traditional digital markets largely required customers to search for, compare, and interact directly with businesses, generative AI systems and emerging AI agents can increasingly retrieve information, synthesize alternatives, generate recommendations, influence consideration sets, initiate transactions, and potentially execute purchases on behalf of users. This transition creates a business-side problem that is not fully captured by existing organizational AI readiness and AI maturity frameworks. This paper proposes AI-Mediated Business Readiness (AMBR) as a conceptual construct describing the degree to which a business possesses the informational, reputational, technological, commercial, and operational conditions required to remain competitive within AI-mediated customer journeys. The framework integrates six stages: Discover, Understand, Trust, Select, Transact, and Deliver. It operationalizes these stages through thirty assessment criteria organized into six dimensions and proposes an evidence-based scoring methodology. The framework does not claim that AI-mediated recommendation, generative search, consumer selection, or agentic commerce are novel phenomena. Existing research has already demonstrated that large language models can participate in recommendation and consumer choice, while emerging research on AI agents demonstrates that agents can evaluate products, exhibit systematic preferences, and affect seller market share. Rather, the proposed contribution is to introduce a business-side, end-to-end readiness perspective that integrates previously fragmented research streams into a single conceptual model. The paper develops the construct, positions it against existing AI readiness, generative search, recommendation, reputation, and agentic commerce literature, proposes an operational assessment model, and formulates research propositions for future empirical validation. The framework is explicitly presented as conceptual and requires subsequent testing for construct validity, reliability, predictive validity, and criterion validity.
why: Business readiness framework, organizational focus.

title: Generative AI in the Banking Sector: Regulatory Mapping
abstract: This report maps the regulatory requirements that credit institutions face when deploying generative AI applications. The analysis covers two regulatory frameworks: the EU AI Act and sectoral banking regulation (CRR, CRD, EBA Guidelines on loan origination and monitoring). Data protection and operational resilience rules fall outside the report's scope, save as noted below. Banking secrecy is treated by reference to Finnish law where it constrains a use case. The report examines four archetypal use cases (employee copilot, customer chatbot, credit decision copilot and credit decision automation) across four deployment modalities (system-as-a-service (SaaS), cloud-based API integration, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) integration and proprietary fine-tuning). Each combination produces a distinct regulatory risk profile. The use case determines overall regulatory intensity, while the value chain position determines the allocation of responsibilities. The employee copilot and customer chatbot are limited-risk AI systems facing transparency obligations only, making compliance achievable. The credit decision copilot is likely a high-risk system whose feasibility is legally uncertain, as supervisors may treat it as de facto automation if the human decision-maker cannot effectively challenge system outputs. Credit decision automation is not feasible under current interpretations, constrained primarily by banking regulation and GDPR explainability requirements rather than the AI Act. In SaaS deployments the financial institution is a deployer and subject to relatively few obligations, while the vendor bears both general purpose AI (GPAI) model and AI system (AIS) provider obligations. In API, RAG and fine-tuning deployments the institution becomes the AIS provider and faces the full AIS provider obligation stack. Standard RAG does not modify model weights and therefore does not push the institution into GPAI model provider status. Fine-tuning triggers GPAI model provider status only in the unlikely case that fine-tuning compute exceeds one-third of the original model's training compute. The explainability gap is the central obstacle. LLMs cannot produce the granular, reproducible and decomposable justifications that banking regulation requires for credit decisions. EBA Guidelines demand that institutions understand the methodology, assumptions and limitations of automated models, while CRR Article 179 requires IRB institutions to break down loss experience by credit risk parameters. Information asymmetry in the GPAI value chain further weakens downstream compliance: the AI Act Code of Practice permits GPAI model providers to reserve bias detection and data quality information for regulators, leaving downstream institutions without the data needed for EBA governance obligations. Additionally, for credit-related use cases, public cloud API deployment creates independent obstacles under banking secrecy and DORA outsourcing requirements, making a private or controlled-cloud environment a necessary prerequisite. Finally, while the AI Act and banking regulation overlap, they do not conflict in formal terms. Both require risk management, data governance, documentation and testing. However, the requirements diverge in emphasis: the AI Act focuses on system-level health, safety and fundamental rights risks, whereas banking regulation focuses on model-level explainability, auditability and historical backtesting.
why: Regulatory mapping reference, survey not original research

title: From Document Review to Evidence-Based Assurance - A Two-Case Applied Study of AI-Assisted Policy Review in Finance and Governance
abstract: This paper examines whether a controlled AI-assisted policy-review workflow can move beyond document generation toward evidence-based assurance in Finance and governance. It uses a two-case applied comparative design based on two real policy reviews undertaken at Cannons Creek Independent School NPC in South Africa: a Financial Management Policy review on 24 August 2026 and a Recruitment Policy review on 25 August 2026. Both cases used the same broad seven-step Policy Review Advisor architecture: document classification, legislative and compliance context, organisational context, an explicitly approved alignment baseline, sourcedocument review, human-approved recommended changes, and a final reviewed document that remained subject to organisational governance approval. Evidence comprised the full conversation/process records, approved alignment profiles, recommendation registers, final reviewed documents, and an OpenAI account data export containing message-level timestamps. Paper 01 recorded 3h 16m 16.409s total elapsed time, of which 5m 21.486s was timestamp-derived AI response time and 3h 7m 7.965s was human-gate latency. Paper 02 recorded 1h 37m 48.510s elapsed, 5m 34.586s AI response time and 1h 29m 38.862s human-gate latency. Paper 02 was 50.17% faster end-to-end even though AI response time was 4.07% longer; the principal difference was 52.09% lower human-gate latency. Qualitative evidence also shows the value of explicit context correction, recommendation approval and controlled escalation: in Paper 02 a remuneration-authority conflict was preserved as unresolved rather than silently decided by the AI. The study does not establish a percentage productivity saving versus manual review, legal compliance, or independent output accuracy because no defensible manual comparator or blind external quality review has yet been performed. The main contribution is an applied demonstration that workflow performance in governed AI work depends not only on model capability, but on context, human decision rights, approval gates, traceability and the operating model around the AI.
why: Policy review workflow, governance not quantitative.

title: Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Entrepreneurship: Economic Performance Analysis and Market Entry Strategies
abstract: Emerging economies marked by institutional deficiencies and elevated informality encounter considerable ambiguity over the impact of digital ecosystems on macroeconomic and entrepreneurial results. This research investigates the correlation between national artificial intelligence (AI) and Big Data ecosystem factors, the absorption of high-tech workers, and overall economic scale within South Asian economies. Utilizing a country-year panel dataset spanning from 2015 to 2025, the analytical approach combines two-way fixed-effects linear regression with an investigative supervised Random Forest regression model. The empirical results indicate that national AI adoption rates by enterprises, AI readiness metrics, and comparative AI market depth show statistically significant positive correlations with the share of AI-related jobs. In contrast, at a fixed total ecosystem scale, an increased concentration of venture capital allocated to AI firms has a detrimental correlation with net AI employment share. In macroeconomic models, short-term fluctuations in digital ecosystem metrics within a country have no statistically significant correlation with overall Gross Domestic Product when baseline national attributes and temporal disturbances are accounted for. Exploratory assessments of feature significance regularly highlight operational business adoption and policy preparedness as key determinants over financial capital contributions. Theoretically, these results broaden the Resource-Based View and institutional theory to the macro-ecosystem scale, suggesting that widespread technological adoption and institutional support are more closely associated with high-tech labor absorption than mere speculative capital concentration. Constrained by its macro country-year analytical framework, the research is unable to determine firm-level survival odds or micro-level founder cognition. This research provides an empirically based, ecosystem-level evaluation illustrating the co-evolution of national digital preparedness and institutional factors with the absorption of high-tech labor markets in emerging economies.
why: Correlational AI adoption, not actionable method.

title: THE SELF-CONTROLLED RECORD OF UNDERWRITING REPRESENTATION Exogenous Fixation and the Rescission Risk in AI Governance Warranties
abstract: In 2022, a cyber insurer obtained a stipulated judgment rescinding a policy ab initio after discovering that its insured had represented enterprise-wide multi-factor authentication at underwriting when the control in fact covered only a firewall. The rescission was not conditioned on any link between the misrepresentation and the ransomware claim that prompted the insurer's inquiry; it turned solely on whether the representation was material to the risk the insurer had agreed to accept. In the aftermath of a widely reported 2026 incident involving autonomous AI agents, a London wholesale broker published nine governance questions it now expects insureds to answer before obtaining affirmative AI coverage — autonomy level, the existence of a formal governance framework, data access and consent scope, monitoring and pre-deployment code review among them — and drew the parallel to the 2022 case explicitly: answering such questions from memory carries the same rescission exposure as misstating a security control. This paper examines what that parallel requires as a matter of evidence. Rescission doctrine asks whether a representation was true when made, a question courts resolve on the facts before them; this paper does not evaluate the truth of any specific representation. It argues instead that several of the governance facts now being underwritten are structurally harder to reconstruct after the fact than a binary control like multi-factor authentication, and that no generally required mechanism identified in the sources examined here fixes what an insured actually declared, and when, through an evidentiary process independent of both the insured's later account and the underwriting system through which the declaration was made. The paper states what an architecture of Exogenous Pre-Execution Fixation could contribute to that specific gap, and what it leaves entirely to the doctrine of materiality to decide.
why: Cyber insurance governance, not financial ML.

title: The Epistemic Liquidity Crisis: Post-2008 Finance and the Political Economy of AI Alignment
abstract: Why did probabilistic optimization come to monopolize AI development while symbolic, causal, and interpretable alternatives were marginalized? Moving beyond model-centric accounts of AI alignment, this article grounds model failures in the political economy of platform infrastructure. We trace a post-2008 convergence in which financial valuation and risk-management rationalities migrated into digital advertising. Real-time bidding platforms institutionalized this transfer, pricing attention at millisecond speeds and subordinating explanation to execution velocity. Within this regime, we reframe two core phenomena, hallucination functions as synthetic epistemic liquidity which is fluent text generated to maintain transactional flow when empirical grounding is absent; Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) operates as a liquidity-management tool that masks model fragility by externalizing volatility onto precarious human annotators. The result is an epistemic liquidity crisis: systems overproduce fluent, confidence-inducing output while their capacity to remain grounded in shared reality fails to keep pace. Ultimately, alignment is a struggle over the political economy of knowledge production. Technical fixes confined to the model layer merely polish the surface, leaving the structural incentives that generate misalignment fully intact.
why: Political economy critique, not actionable.

title: Machine Learning-Based Real-Time Credit Card Fraud Detection
abstract: Credit card fraud is a common occurrence that leads to substantial financial losses [1]. Online shopping has grown in popularity, and the volume of transactions has expanded significantly. A large percentage of these purchases are made using credit cards. Banks and other financial institutions consequently offer services. Software for detecting credit card fraud is quite useful. demand. Transactions that are fraudulent can take many different forms. They fall into a number of categories. This study focusses on four primary instances of fraud in actual transactions. To fight fraud, a number of machine learning models are employed. The best approach is selected through an examination. This evaluation provides you with a methodical strategy to choosing the best business. We illustrate the evaluation with respect to the kinds of frauds and the proper approach with a suitable performance. Another crucial component of our project is the real-time detection of credit card fraud. Therefore, in order to ascertain whether a machine learning model and an API module are suitable, we take into consideration the application of predictive analytics. Is a particular transaction real or fake? Additionally, we assess a novel method for handling the skewed data distribution. According to an open source and community-maintained website, the data we used for our study comes from a range of sources.
why: Generic fraud detection, no rigor or baselines.

title: Algorithmic Litigation Finance and Civil Justice Market Integrity
abstract: Civil litigation is increasingly becoming a financial market in which claims are identified, screened, valued, funded, insured, bundled, settled, and monetised. Third-party litigation finance has already generated policy concern around disclosure, funder identity, settlement influence, litigation control, foreign funding, class actions, and mass torts. Artificial intelligence intensifies these concerns by making claim origination, damages modelling, settlement prediction, document review, demand generation, and portfolio investment faster, cheaper, and less visible. This article argues that litigation finance transparency must therefore evolve into algorithmic litigation finance accountability. Building on the author’s parent proposal, The Civil Justice Integrity Screening Framework for Litigation Abuse and Institutional Accountability, this article develops the finance-facing branch of that broader civil justice integrity project. It proposes the Algorithmic Litigation Finance Accountability Framework, a seven-domain model for evaluating AI-enabled litigation finance across claim origination integrity, funding transparency, algorithmic control risk, portfolio distortion risk, evidence and damages reliability, settlement pressure and bargaining fairness, and access-to-justice protection. The article then operationalises the framework through the Algorithmic Funding Disclosure and Integrity Test, a five-question assessment tool designed to identify whether an AI-enabled litigation finance arrangement appears legitimate or low-risk, moderate-risk, high-risk, or in need of enhanced human review. The article further recommends future development of the Algorithmic Funding Disclosure, AI Assessment, and Integrity Classification Model as an AI-assisted, human-governed system for structured intake, supporting-document classification, provisional AI pre-assessment, evidence and damages traceability, risk classification, red-flag detection, human-review routing, report generation, auditability, and scalable implementation. A companion preregistered protocol, Feasibility and Scalability Protocol for Algorithmic Legal Finance Integrity, specifies the planned stakeholder validation, data collection, reliability assessment, and methodological requirements that will precede working-model development and controlled model testing. The companion protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework under embargo before data collection.
why: Litigation finance policy; not operational ML method.

title: Deleveraging When Investors Trade Again
abstract: A clearing institution that must terminate a fixed quantity of contracts has to decide which accounts bear the reduction. We study whether knowing subsequent trading is enough to choose the allocation minimizing expected account funding shortfalls. In a three-participant economy, we construct two cash-buffer states with identical prices, trades and positions under every allocation on a common regular equilibrium branch. Their shortfall objectives are strictly convex but have different unique minimizers. Counterparty cash changes the states requiring replenishment without changing unconstrained demand. We characterize when this missing cash state leaves a feasible allocation derivative unchanged. Under additional one-factor tail conditions, a unique cash threshold separates opposite local priorities when the counterparty's marginal shortfall contribution crosses the other accounts' benefit. With a known payoff distribution, the counterparty's shortfall cutoff supplies the missing state information. Equal fixed-price retention shares yield a separable, strictly convex benchmark on a fully regular allocation domain. The common-map construction also persists under a class of small nonnormal payoff perturbations. The criterion measures terminal account replenishment under stated settlement conditions. The results distinguish information needed to predict trading from information needed to evaluate funding consequences, within the specified branches and observation set. Declaration of generative AI use The author used OpenAI Codex for language polishing and routine software engineering support, including writing repetitive code and assisting with computational implementation. The research design, theoretical arguments, and interpretation of results were reviewed by the author, who takes full responsibility for the final manuscript.
why: Microstructure theory, pure math, no data.

title: Machine-Learning-Based Anomaly Detection in Accounting Data: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly proposed for detecting anomalies in accounting data, yet the research remains fragmented and lacks a synthesis that reflects the specific characteristics of this domain. This study presents a systematic literature review of 22 studies on ML-based anomaly detection in financial accounting data, focusing on journal entries and the general ledger. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the corpus is analyzed from three perspectives: theory, methodology, and empirical evidence. Theoretically, the literature conceptualizes anomalies as audit leads that indicate potential misstatements rather than as direct evidence of fraud or error. However, audit semantics such as materiality are rarely integrated into model design and evaluation, leaving a semantic gap between statistical deviations and audit-relevant irregularities. Methodologically, the field is concentrated: autoencoder-based architectures dominate unsupervised detection and tree-based classifiers dominate supervised detection, while the central burden lies in transforming structurally rich, high-cardinality, and highly imbalanced journal data into ML-compatible representations without losing audit-relevant meaning. Empirically, the evidence rests largely on single-company, single-fiscal-year case studies using proprietary SAP-derived data; only 7 of 38 datasets and 4 of 22 code bases are publicly available, which limits reproducibility and comparability. We conclude that the principal bottleneck of the field is not a lack of modeling ideas but the absence of a shared semantic and empirical foundation. Based on these findings, we derive a research agenda comprising conceptual foundations, preprocessing guidelines, hybrid detection systems, human-AI interaction, and a shared benchmark infrastructure to advance ML-based anomaly detection toward audit-useful practice.
why: ML anomaly detection review, literature synthesis.

title: Open-Source AI and Market Competition: Why the United Kingdom Is Well Placed to Promote Openness as Competition Policy
abstract: The generative artificial intelligence industry is consolidating around a small number of proprietary model developers and their hyperscaler partners. This article argues that open-source and open-weight models can provide an important structural constraint on that tendency by lowering entry barriers, disciplining price and non-price terms, widening downstream choice and reducing dependence on a single model provider. It develops a layered competition analysis in which rivalry at the model layer can coexist with market power in compute, cloud and digital distribution. It then argues that the United Kingdom is particularly well placed to preserve this constraint. Part 1 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 can prevent strategic gateways from neutralising rival models, while the absence of general model-layer duties keeps entry comparatively open. Public compute and procurement can complement enforcement by lowering supply-side barriers and creating routes to deployment. Because openness is a spectrum, public support should be calibrated to the competitive value actually created rather than to an 'open' label alone. For antitrust enforcement, the implication is to protect the conditions in which open alternatives can compete rather than to protect openness as a category.
why: AI competition policy, regulatory position paper, no empirical contribution

title: The Strategic Imperative of Credit Union Relevance | Petar Jelinic The Strategic Imperative of Credit Union Relevance Translating Cooperative Identity into Recognizable Member and Community Value
abstract: Credit unions occupy a distinctive position in the U.S. financial system because their cooperative structure combines financial intermediation with member ownership and a community-oriented purpose. Yet institutional purpose does not automatically produce continuing relevance. Relevance must be experienced through accessible products, responsive service, responsible credit, trusted relationships, digital capability, community presence, and governance decisions that translate cooperative identity into contemporary value. This article argues that the central strategic challenge for credit unions is not whether the cooperative model remains valuable, but whether individual institutions can continually convert that model into outcomes that members and communities can recognize and use. Current system data illustrate both strength and pressure. Federally insured credit unions held approximately $2.48 trillion in assets and served 145.8 million members in the first quarter of 2026, while the number of federally insured institutions declined from 4,411 to 4,250 over the preceding year (National Credit Union Administration [NCUA], 2026). The article develops an integrated framework of member, digital, economic, community, generational, and institutional relevance and considers leadership, culture, governance, artificial intelligence, responsible lending, and financial inclusion as mechanisms through which relevance can be sustained. The analysis concludes that cooperative identity becomes strategically consequential only when it is converted into measurable and repeatedly experienced value.
why: Credit union strategy paper, organizational focus.

title: European Digital Sovereignty: Data, Cloud Capital and the European Single Market
abstract: Europe faces a crisis of digital sovereignty. On the economic side, The 2025 Annual EU Single Market and Competitiveness Report published by the European Commission presents a Europe that is uncompetitive, slow and falling behind on digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence. To this end, the solution supported by the Commission is to ‘simplify’ the EU acquis (European Commission, 2025d). At the same time, political scandals like Cambridge Analytica and the information released in the Epstein Files arouse suspicions of coordinated interference within European and national elections (Monteleone, 2019) and conducting operations to strengthen support for far-right candidates across the continent (Il Fatto Quotidiano, 2026). From the perspective of digital sovereignty, this study utilises the concept of cloud capital to analyse the EU’s approach to legislating ‘big tech’, evidencing the strengths of the current European law system in ensuring digital sovereignty, its weaknesses, and suggest possible improvements.
why: European tech policy, off-topic from finance.

title: Beyond AI Adoption: Creating Business Value in Financial Services
abstract: How financial institutions are moving from AI experimentation to measurable business outcomes "AI is no longer a differentiator in financial services. The competitive advantage now lies in how effectively institutions transform AI capabilities into better decisions, stronger customer relationships, improved compliance, and measurable business outcomes.
why: Position paper, no substantive content.

title: Digital Economics Firms, Markets, Platforms, Data, and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: These lecture notes explore the evolution of the digital economy toward an integrated economy of architectures. The author reformulates the traditional circular flow model by distinguishing real, monetary, informational, and algorithmic flows. By analyzing multi-sided platforms, the text examines how private actors design market rules, matching mechanisms, and data access. It revisits the Coasian theory of the firm under the influence of generative artificial intelligence and autonomous agentic systems. Organizational design is analyzed through the jagged technological frontier, highlighting the need for strategic human-AI complementarities. The manuscript details infrastructural concentration across consecutive layers of hardware, hyperscale cloud computing, and foundation models. It addresses the economic implications of data governance, privacy rights, and functional portability under Chile's new regulatory frameworks. The text demystifies the immateriality of digital abundance by incorporating the material, energy, and water footprint of AI. Special focus is given to Latin America, illustrating productive AIoT applications in commodities like mining and precision agriculture. Ultimately, the role of engineers is redefined from technical coders to mechanism architects capable of designing sustainable ecosystems.
why: Lecture notes and survey, not research.

title: Crude oil arbitrage and momentum trading strategies with targeting volatility by using Large Language Models
abstract: This paper is devoted to the execution of crude oil arbitrage and momentum strategies with volatility targeting by using Large Language Models (LLM), comparing efficiency and profitability of LLaMA2 and GPT3.5. The objective of this study is to estimate the impacts of oil price volatility on oil companies' strategic investments from a regional level. Therefore, oil price volatility should be an independent variable in the model equation. This method is consistent with earlier studies that investigate the relationship between uncertainty and investment in Tobin's q theory. Oil price uncertainty can arise from a number of different sources including global oil demand and supply conditions, the actions of institutional actors (OPEC), geopolitical issues (approximately 50 per cent of world proven oil reserves are located in just four countries in the Middle East), and speculation in oil future markets. The complicated elements contribute the oil price uncertainty to be high and hard to predict. Therefore, although high oil prices normally imply high profits for oil exploration and production companies, the uncertainty of price could still significantly impact their strategic investment decisions. Previous studies diversify their results in the shape of the relationship between oil price uncertainty and investment.
