For instance, studies such as Mohn & Misund (2009) and Elder & Serietis (2010) find a linear relationship between oil price uncertainty and investment; while Henriques & Sadorsky (2011) found a Ucurve relationship. Therefore, in this study, the variable of oil price volatility square will be introduced as an optional variable. If the specification of model with the variable shows a better result than the one without it, then the shape of the relationship would be a curve line. Volatility targeting is a portfolio management tool aimed at managing portfolio risk by targeting a particular volatility level and adjusting the positioning of the portfolio in an attempt to stay close to the volatility target. Although it is possible to implement volatility targeting with any asset, portfolios of derivatives provide a cost-effective implementation as trading is often done on a daily basis. Following the research of Moreira and Muir (2017) the idea is very straightforward; one needs to simply scale asset weights in the portfolio by the ratio of the target volatility and the expectation of future volatility given the current asset mix. Obviously, the value of the targeting is greatly impacted by the quality of the volatility expectation model, but since these estimates are over short horizons, the fact that volatility tends to cluster makes this an "easier" effort. In equation form, the return of the volatility managed portfolio, is the volatility scaled return of the unmanaged portfolio which is simply the sum product of the asset weights and their returns. Crude oil is a pivotal global commodity whose price fluctuations permeate the broader economy through channels such as transportation costs, energy-weighted inflation indices, and corporate procurement and inventory strategies. Accurate forecasting of oil prices, even for single-step daily predictions, holds significant practical value. Marginal but consistent accuracy gains around price turning points can substantially mitigate risks associated with supply disruptions and excessive hedging costs. However, the inherent characteristics of oil markets-such as fat-tailed residuals, volatility clustering, asymmetric responses to supply and demand shocks, and frequent structural breaks-pose considerable challenges to traditional linear models. While classical time series approaches like ARIMA and exponential smoothing capture low-frequency trends, they often fall short in modeling the complex, nonlinear interactions among inventory levels, convenience yields, market expectations, and geopolitical risks. Although regime-switching models introduce nonlinearity, their reliance on strong assumptions regarding the number of states and transition mechanisms limits their applicability during unconventional events. From a methodological viewpoint, I improved on existing approaches to pairs trading by assessing the cointegration among the three futures prices at the same time and modeling the resulting cointegration spread by a mean-reverting process with regime-switching modulated by a hidden Markov chain. title: Pricing in the Age of AI: What Every Business Leader Needs to Know
abstract: AI is transforming one of the oldest and most consequential decisions in business. The opportunity is not simply to automate pricing, but to make it more intelligent, adaptive, and personalized. AI allows companies to analyze more data, experiment with prices at scale, and adjust decisions dynamically, while generative AI makes sophisticated pricing capabilities accessible through natural language. Yet these advances also create new challenges. Pricing recommendations can depend heavily on the data, model, and prompts, and the most profitable price may not always be the right one when fairness, trust, and regulation are considered. Importantly, human judgment remains essential. Drawing on my recent book, Pricing in the Age of AI, as well as research and real-world examples, this article examines how AI is reshaping pricing and offers five rules to help executives use it effectively and responsibly: experiment continuously, use AI as a copilot, treat the prompt as part of the pricing system, keep humans accountable, and optimize for trust, not just profit.
why: Business leadership position paper on AI pricing, no research

title: Business Value of Integrated Physical, Digital, and Information Security in Egyptian Food Logistics A Reproducible Monte Carlo Portfolio Study
abstract: Food logistics security is often managed through separate investments in physical controls, cybersecurity, information governance, supplier assurance, cold-chain monitoring, and continuity preparedness. This paper treats these controls as a portfolio whose business value depends on expected loss, tail risk, and service continuity. A reproducible Monte Carlo design generated 1,200 feasible security allocations subject to a fixed budget. Each portfolio was evaluated against synthetic theft, tampering, cyber, information-integrity, supplier, cold-chain, and disruption risks. Expected loss ranged from 22.64 to 37.96 index points, while conditional value at risk at the 95th percentile ranged from 132.86 to 222.46. The selected compromise portfolio allocated 12.6% to physical security, 22.0% to cybersecurity, 20.4% to information governance, 13.3% to supplier assurance, 14.5% to cold-chain monitoring, and 17.2% to continuity preparedness. It achieved expected loss of 22.77, CVaR95 of 132.86, and service continuity of 84.74. Only two portfolios lay on the strict efficient frontier, showing that small allocation changes can alter the balance between average loss, extreme loss, and continuity. The analysis demonstrates a transparent risk-return method; it does not estimate actual Egyptian firms or incidents. AI use disclosure. Generative AI tools assisted with language drafting, document formatting, and programming support. Farouk Eldakhlawy is responsible for independently verifying the research design, assumptions, code, numerical outputs, citations, figures, interpretations, and final text and for approving any version submitted or publicly posted.

title: From Attraction to Embedding: A Comparative Analysis of Human Capital Policies for R&D+I in the GCC and Singapore
abstract: Gulf Cooperation Council states have substantially expanded research investment over the past decade, establishing dedicated research authorities and increasing researcher numbers; in Saudi Arabia, researcher density more than doubled between 2020 and 2024. Innovation outputs have not followed. Every GCC state ranks materially lower on the output measures of the Global Innovation Index than on its input measures; high-technology goods account for between zero and three per cent of exports in five of the six states across the fifteen years from 2010, and academic-corporate collaboration has not exceeded five per cent of regional research output. This divergence is documented in the existing literature; the mechanism behind it is not. This paper examines talent policy as one candidate explanation, in economies where non-nationals hold roughly four-fifths of employment and all foreign residents are classified in law as temporary regardless of length of stay. It develops a three-dimensional framework — attraction, retention and embedding — and applies it to all six GCC states individually, with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates examined in depth and Singapore serving as comparator. Evidence is drawn from national statistical sources, international indicators, and primary legal and policy documents including the Saudi Premium Residency Permit Law, UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 29 of 2021, and Singapore's Ministry of Manpower and A*STAR scheme documentation. The findings differ by dimension. Attraction has succeeded: the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia both recorded higher net inflows of artificial intelligence talent than Singapore in 2025. Retention cannot be assessed through outcomes, since no published study has measured how long foreign researchers remain in any of the seven cases; assessed through instrument design, both available routes are closed in the Gulf, as researchers are admitted without a pathway to membership while workforce localisation programmes exempt the positions they occupy. The cases separate most clearly on embedding, and on a measure of ownership rather than employment: between eighty and ninety per cent of GCC patent applications are filed by individuals rather than companies, the reverse of the proportion in industrialised economies, against ninety-two per cent of granted patents held by private firms in Singapore. Attraction and embedding are separable achievements, and the Gulf states have secured the first without the second. A transferability assessment applying Dolowitz and Marsh's framework finds that the instruments easiest to adopt depend most heavily on conditions the Gulf states currently lack, while those requiring no institutional groundwork lie outside the reach of talent policy. The paper contributes a comparison at the instrument level between two settings the literature has treated separately, an account of institutional variation within the region that bloc-level analysis obscures, and the identification of a measurable evidence gap.
why: R&D policy research, not financial markets.

title: AI-DRIVEN SUSTAINABLE INFRASTRUCTURE: MACHINE LEARNING, ESG METRICS, AND LOW-CARBON CONCRETE OPTIMIZATION
abstract: The construction sector is a major contributor to global greenhouse-gas emissions and resource consumption, representing a critical target for decarbonization and resilience efforts. Integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into infrastructure decision-making increases transparency and long-term value but introduces complexity due to data heterogeneity and multi-stakeholder objectives. This paper examines the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, Bayesian inference, and multi-objective optimization, to optimize sustainable construction systems while explicitly incorporating ESG metrics. Methods for emissions and cost forecasting, uncertainty quantification, adaptive design optimization, and trade-off analysis are synthesized, with a quantified case example in low-carbon concrete mix design, using a linear optimization model to estimate emissions-reduction potential under realistic mix-design constraints. Principal challenges such as ESG data uncertainty, model interpretability, and scalability are discussed, and actionable recommendations are proposed, including standardized ESG reporting, adoption of explainable AI, hybrid ML-LCA workflows, and policy incentives to de-risk innovation. By aligning AI methods with ESG frameworks, this approach advances resilient, economically viable, and verifiably sustainable infrastructure practice.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cross-Federation Application Placement in Edge-Cloud Prosumer Markets
abstract: Application placement across the multi-tenant edge–cloud continuum remains suboptimal, as various providers struggle to coordinate provisioning for efficient resource access across administrative domains. Resource federations can mitigate this fragmentation by enabling providers to pool heterogeneous resources and jointly orchestrate their allocation. However, modern applications' requirements cannot be addressed through small-scale unification alone and require provisioning across multiple federations. In this work, we consider a multi-federation computing substrate and introduce a coordination framework for cross-federation inter-operation. We formulate the problem as a prosumer market where federations are incentivized to dynamically procure or lease out resources depending on demand and scarcity conditions. Coordination is realized through a dynamic multi-dimensional reverse auction that jointly determines the offered resource configuration and its lease price. The framework accounts for competition at both the federation and constituent provider levels, jointly optimizing latency, federation profitability and equitable profit distribution. Market interactions are formulated as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game with federations as self-interested agents. To handle the high-dimensional action space, we introduce MA3PO-SAC, a Multi-Agent Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning architecture that decomposes bidding into specialized networks for discrete resource selection and continuous pricing. Trace-driven experiments using the Google Borg trace and cloud-calibrated infrastructure configurations demonstrate that MA3PO-SAC learns adaptive bidding attuned to market conditions and to both individual and peer objectives. The method outperforms alternative MARL baselines and achieves system welfare within 3\% of a centralized full-visibility orchestrator, despite partial observability, inter-federation competition, and decentralized control.
why: Edge-cloud infrastructure, off-topic.

title: Learning to Price and Pool: Reinforcement Learning for Joint Pricing and Solo-Pooled Driver Assignment in Ride-hailing Systems
abstract: Ride-hailing platforms that offer both private and pooled ride-hailing services must jointly determine how to allocate their available fleet between the two services and how to price each. These two decisions are inherently interdependent: rider choices between private and pooled ride-hailing depend jointly on the fares and expected service conditions of each option, while those conditions are in turn shaped by how available drivers are allocated across services. Notwithstanding, past studies, have largely optimized pricing and service-type assignment separately, considered only a single service type, or treated the vehicle service mix as fixed rather than as a decision that can be adjusted in real time as demand evolves. This study addresses this gap by proposing a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that jointly and dynamically optimizes pricing and vehicle-level service-type assignment under endogenous, choice-based rider demand, modeled using a utility-based discrete-choice model. We formulate the problem as a multi-agent Markov Decision Process and train a pricing agent together with a service-type assignment agent using a cooperative PPO-based training algorithm within a purpose-built ride-hailing simulation environment. To scale to large, variable-size fleets without a corresponding increase in the number of model parameters, the service-type agent adopts a parameter-sharing architecture across vehicles. Experiments on the Delft and Amsterdam road networks, with fleets of up to 1,000 vehicles, show that the proposed framework learns stable, coordinated pricing and service-type assignment policies that achieve higher revenue and cumulative return than rule-based and single-component learning baselines, while remaining responsive to shifts in market scale and rider preferences. An ablation study further shows that parameter sharing reduces training time by roughly 22\% relative to a non-sharing variant.

title: A Stochastic Feasibility and Optimization Model for Self-Financing AI Adoption in Rural Pathology Under Medicare Reimbursement Constraints
abstract: Existing literature reports that AI-assisted pathology workflows can increase pathologist throughput by factors ranging from 1.16 to 1.84, corresponding to approximately 16% to 84% greater diagnostic capacity in the workflows studied. Despite reported efficiency gains, adoption of AI-enabled digital pathology remains limited in community and rural settings, where financial, infrastructure, and workforce constraints can impede implementation. We developed a stochastic financial feasibility model that links AI-driven productivity gains in urban pathology departments to performance-linked incremental-revenue sharing, rural pathology capacity, pathologist compensation, and Critical Access Hospital infrastructure costs. The model evaluates whether AI financing, rural compensation sufficiency, and rural infrastructure cost recovery can be achieved simultaneously under uncertainty in parameters derived from federal datasets, published literature, and explicit modeling assumptions. In 50,000 Monte Carlo simulations parameterized using federal datasets, published literature, and explicit modeling assumptions, joint feasibility was achieved in 41.4% of simulations. The model required a minimum efficiency multiplier of 1.165 and produced a five-year combined hospital-and-AI-vendor net present value of $52.45 million under base-case assumptions. Importantly, the proposed mechanism is constructed using existing re-imbursement categories and potentially available federal grant mechanisms and does not assume creation of a new AI-specific Medicare payment program.
